title: "Brain slice visualization via the grammar of graphics"
format: html

## Introduction
Data visualization serves as the foundation for all scientific communication, and in the field of neuroscience, brain visualization serves as a central tool for the communication of research findings, creating grounds for vast software options to visualize brain images. Voxel-type visualization software commonly used by neuroscientists inlude ANTsR, ANTsPy, fsbrain, and RMINC, with the landscape ranging from straightforward to use while offering only specific plot types, to very complex visualization techniques for more flexible plotting of brain images, giving the user more control over the representation of the data. 

A middle ground can be found by employing the Grammar of Graphics (GoG) framework where brain images can be very flexibly plotted. In R, ```ggplot2``` is a data visualization framework based on the GoG. Similarly, the ```plotnine``` package offers the same tools as ```ggplot2``` in Python. By providing voxel-wise data in a tidy data frame, ```ggplot2``` can present data after mapping a series of aesthetics and primitives. With the fundamental ideas of the GoG, complex visualizations and images can be generated by understanding how to layer each aesthetic and primitive, beyond basic charts and graphs. Complex images, such as atlas' overlayed on a brain image, can be created by ```ggplot2``` and ```plotnine```, which are versatile in displaying brain images beyond standard sagittal, coronal, and axial views, by understanding the GoG. 

?A basic rundown of the Grammar of Graphics?

The advantages of using a Grammar of Graphics method of neuroimaging visualization is its seamless integration into the normal programming workflows that already use R and/or Python for data analysis and its versitality in producing any type of plot, from annotations to layering atlases. By harnessing the built-in framework found in ```gglot2``` and/or ```plotnine```, the workflow from data analysis to brain visualization no longer requires the use of multiple software options. With this, one can have make complex visuals from making multi-slice plots, annotated slices, and layering atlases all in one workspace that is not provided by many other packges.

The disadvantages of utilizing this framework arises mainly from the slightest learning curve that comes with learning the language of the Grammar of Graphics and a requirement that the imaging data, including coordinates and voxel intensities, must be processed into a data frame in order to use the GoG framework provided by ```ggplot2``` or ```plotnine```. However, both this tutorial and a new image data processing package, 'ggslicer', were developped to address both those issues. This tutorial will provide a simple overview of a range of possible visualizations so that one may get comfortable with the framework. In addition, the 'ggslicer' package was developed with the purpose of processing images to return a dataframe with all the necessary information to use ```ggplot2``` and ```plotnine```.

A tutorial for this method of voxel-type, code-based visualization is outlined below. The tutorial is presented in R with ```ggplot2``` and in Python with the equivalent package ```plotnine```.

## Tutorial
# Prepare environment and load the data
To start, we will need to load or install the following packages in an R environment:

* ```tidyverse``` (metapackage)
* ```glue```
* ```scales```
* ```ggnewscale```
* ```patchwork```

or the following in a Python environment:

* ```plotnine```
* ```pandas```
* ```scales```
* ```ggnewscale```
* ```patchworklib```

In addition, we will require SimpleITK installed on your system and the development version of 'ggslicer', which can be found in the following GitHub repository: <https://github.com/shanafu/ggslicer>

The data we will use in this tutorial will be the mni space template, which can also be found in the GitHub repository above in the "tutorial" folder.

With the environment prepared, let us have a look at the data. The functions in ```ggslicer``` all require image data which we will determine to be the mni space template. Then, we can use ```ggslicer```'s functions to view the image data in a processed "long" data table.

```r
image <- "mni_icbm152_t1_tal_nlin_sym_09c.mnc"

coordinates <- slice_axis(image, "x", c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60))
```
The function ```slice_axis()``` formats the image data into a data table with columns displaying the orientation and the coordinates we selected. If none were specified, all the coordinates of the image would be displayed. To view the data table, simply type ```coordinates``` or you can also ```View(coordinates)```.
```
     x   y   z  i   j k slice_axis slice_index slice_world
1   10  96 -78 86   0 0          x           1          10
2   10  95 -78 86   1 0          x           1          10
3   10  94 -78 86   2 0          x           1          10
4   10  93 -78 86   3 0          x           1          10
5   10  92 -78 86   4 0          x           1          10
6   10  91 -78 86   5 0          x           1          10
7   10  90 -78 86   6 0          x           1          10
8   10  89 -78 86   7 0          x           1          10
9   10  88 -78 86   8 0          x           1          10
10  10  87 -78 86   9 0          x           1          10
 [ reached 'max' / getOption("max.print") -- omitted 265172 rows ]
```

There is also a ```slice_intensity``` function that appends the intensity values of each voxel into a data frame format.
```r
intensities <- slice_intensity(image, coordinates)
```
To view the data table, simply type ```intensities``` or you can also ```View(intensities)```.
```
    intensity  x  y   z  i  j k slice_axis slice_index slice_world
1    17.39497 10 96 -78 86  0 0          x           1          10
2    18.89774 10 95 -78 86  1 0          x           1          10
3    20.53957 10 94 -78 86  2 0          x           1          10
4    22.69907 10 93 -78 86  3 0          x           1          10
5    25.20754 10 92 -78 86  4 0          x           1          10
6    27.31425 10 91 -78 86  5 0          x           1          10
7    28.38820 10 90 -78 86  6 0          x           1          10
8    29.94119 10 89 -78 86  7 0          x           1          10
9    31.48516 10 88 -78 86  8 0          x           1          10
10   31.68733 10 87 -78 86  9 0          x           1          10
 [ reached 'max' / getOption("max.print") -- omitted 265172 rows ]
```
As you see above, the data table (in R, often called a ```tibble``` or ```data.frame```) contains not just the voxel values (under column labeled ```intensity```) but also the associated world coordinates along with some additional data on the slice and whether the selected voxel lies within a brain mask.

Normally, this is an inefficient way of storing data due these extra columns requiring additional memory that could be saved if the data were represented in other ways. In visualizing via the grammar of graphics framework however, there is value to representing the data in this way: we are able to map and scale values based on columns, which turns out to be a powerful tool in creating custom brain images. Besides, with modern computers, the additional memory footprint of representing imaging data in this manner will almost certainly not be a problem.

# A simple plot
To start, let’s plot only a single slice of the brain. First, we will rename our example data earlier and subset the data to only include one slice:
```r 
r
df_template <- intensities

df_template_singleslice <- df_template %>%
    filter(x==10)
```
```python
python

df_template_singleslice = df_template[df_template["x"] == 10]
```
How do we plot with ggplot? Very simple: 

1. Define the data source (```df_template_singleslice```) and specify the mapping. We are plotting sagittal slices, so we want to x-axis of the plot to be associated with the y-coordinate and the y-axis of the plot to be associated with the z-coordinate.
2. Pick the geometry (here, we want the raster geom) and add that as a layer, specifying that we should fill the raster value based on the ```intensity``` column.

```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice,
        mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
    geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"))
)
```
![](/simpleplot1.png)
**Note:** Each layer gets its own data, mapping, and geometry.

```geom_raster``` looks for data and required mappings. If it can’t find what it needs, it inherits it from the main ```ggplot``` plot object.

```ggplot``` is a generic plotting framework and wasn’t specifically designed from brains, so somethings might look “off”. We’ll have to tweak a few things to make our brain image better.

First, ```ggplot``` scales the axes to fit the plotting area. When plotting brain slices, the axes represent physical coordinates at a specific resolution. Let’s fix the coordinates to have the same scale on both the x- and y-axes:
```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice,
            mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
    geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity)) +
    coord_fixed(ratio=1)
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"))
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
)
```
![](/simpleplot2.png)
Next, usually prefer other colour schemes. This can be changed by modifying the default scale to a custom one. Here, we’ll specify the mapping who’s scale we want to modify (```scale_fill_*```) and explicitly add our own gradient scale (```scale_fill_gradient```):
```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice,
            mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
    geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity)) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white') +
    coord_fixed(ratio=1)
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"))
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white")
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
)
```
![](/simpleplot3.png)

# Customizing your plot
Each ```geom``` has its own set of options, and ```geom_raster``` can optionally linearly interpolate. To see these effects, we have to really zoom in, which we will do by filtering the data to only include voxels within a smaller square. Let’s look at plots without and with interpolation:
```r
r

df_template_singleslice_zoomedin <- df_template_singleslice %>% filter(y > -10, y < 20, z > -10, z < 20)

plt_without_interpolation <- ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice_zoomedin,
                                    mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate=F) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1)

plt_with_interpolation <- ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice_zoomedin,
                                    mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate=T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1)

plt_without_interpolation + plt_with_interpolation
```
```python
python

df_template_singleslice_zoomedin = df_template_singleslice[
    (df_template_singleslice["y"] > -10)
    & (df_template_singleslice["y"] < 20)
    & (df_template_singleslice["z"] > -10)
    & (df_template_singleslice["z"] < 20)
]

plt_without_interpolation = (
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice_zoomedin, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation=None)
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
)

plt_with_interpolation = (
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice_zoomedin, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
)

# Using patchworklib syntax for side-by-side plotting:
patchworklib.load_ggplot(plt_without_interpolation) + patchworklib.load_ggplot(plt_with_interpolation)
```
![](/customize1.png)
While we’re zoomed in, it’s also worth pointing out that the geometry is independent of the data and mapping - for example, we can use geom_point instead of geom_raster. Let’s compare the two:
```r
r

plt_with_raster <- ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice_zoomedin,
                                    mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate=F) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) 

plt_with_point <- ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice_zoomedin,
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_point(mapping=aes(color=intensity), size=1) +
  scale_color_gradient(low='black', high='white') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1)

plt_with_raster + plt_with_point
```
```python
python

plt_with_raster = (
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice_zoomedin, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation=None)
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white")
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
)

plt_with_point = (
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice_zoomedin, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_point(mapping=aes(color="intensity"), size=1)
    + scale_color_gradient(low="black", high="white")
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
)

patchworklib.load_ggplot(plt_with_raster) + patchworklib.load_ggplot(plt_with_point)
```
![](/customize2.png)
Scales and guides are customizable too. Let’s increase the contrast by making the range smaller using the limits option. By default, values outside this range won’t be plotted. We’ll instead force these values to be rendered with the colour at the limit using the out of bounds ```oob``` option. Lastly, we’ll also remove the guide, since the intensity values are arbitrary.

```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice,
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1)
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
)
```
![](/customize3.png)
We can further customize other elements of the plot, from axes titles to the overall theme. ```ggplot``` provides several themes (and you can create your own). Let’s switch to a black and white theme (```theme_bw```) and relabel the axes using ```xlab``` and ```ylab``` (by default, the axes titles come from the mappings, i.e. column names within the data, which we specified):
```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice,
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  xlab("Posterior-Anterior") +
  ylab("Inferior-Superior") +
  theme_bw() 
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + xlab("Posterior-Anterior")
    + ylab("Inferior-Superior")
    + theme_bw()
)
```
![](/customize4.png)
In most cases, we don’t want the panel grid and axes. We can remove these outright by switching to an extremely minimal theme, ```theme_void```:
```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice,
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  xlab("Posterior-Anterior") +
  ylab("Inferior-Superior") +
  theme_void()
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + xlab("Posterior-Anterior")
    + ylab("Inferior-Superior")
    + theme_void()
)
```
![](/customize5.png)
As mentioned earlier, everything is customizable, and we can override theme specifications, which we’ll do to add just the axes titles back...
```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice,
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  xlab("Posterior-Anterior") +
  ylab("Inferior-Superior") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.title=element_text(size=10))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + xlab("Posterior-Anterior")
    + ylab("Inferior-Superior")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(axis_title=element_text(size=10))
)
```
![](/customize6.png)
... and rotate the y-axis title:
```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice,
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  xlab("Posterior-Anterior") +
  ylab("Inferior-Superior") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.title=element_text(size=10),
        axis.title.y = element_text(angle=90))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_singleslice, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + xlab("Posterior-Anterior")
    + ylab("Inferior-Superior")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(
        axis_title=element_text(size=10),
        axis_title_y=element_text(angle=90)
    )
)
```
![](/customize7.png)
As you can see above where we only provided ```axis.title.y``` with an angle, theme specifications are also inherited; it is getting all other necessary information from ```axis.title``` and ```theme_void```. 

This means that order matters; if you put ```theme_void``` after your own theme specifications (```... + theme(...) + theme_void()```), then ```theme_void``` would override what you’ve provided in ```theme()```.

# Multi-slice plots
So far we’ve only plotted a single slice. In the original data frame, data for other slices exist. Let us subset our slices to the coordinates 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60, and then observe the number of rows associated with each unique value in slice_world, i.e. number of voxels in each slice:
```r
table(df_template$slice_world)
```
```
   10    20    30    40    50    60 
44197 44197 44197 44197 44197 44197 
```
If we were to replace the data in our plotting code above with this data frame instead, we get a single slice image back:

```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template,
       mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  xlab("Posterior-Anterior") +
  ylab("Inferior-Superior") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.title=element_text(size=10),
        axis.title.y = element_text(angle=90))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + xlab("Posterior-Anterior")
    + ylab("Inferior-Superior")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(
        axis_title=element_text(size=10),
        axis_title_y=element_text(angle=90)
    )
)
```
![](/multi1.png)
Why? We haven’t told ```ggplot``` how to handle the different slices. In fact, all slices are indeed being plotted with raster values being placed at the correct locations, but with different slices. These values are being plotted on top of each other! 

We can see this by reversing the order of the data in the data frame, which causes ```ggplot``` to reverse the order in which the data are laid onto the plot, and effectively results in us seeing a sagittal slice at the other end of the left-right axis instead.
```r
r

ggplot(data=(df_template %>% arrange(slice_world)),
       mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  xlab("Posterior-Anterior") +
  ylab("Inferior-Superior") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.title=element_text(size=10),
        axis.title.y = element_text(angle=90))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template.sort_values("slice_world"), mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + xlab("Posterior-Anterior")
    + ylab("Inferior-Superior")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(
        axis_title=element_text(size=10),
        axis_title_y=element_text(angle=90)
    )
)
```
![](/multi2.png)
So how do we view multiple slices? Using facets. ```ggplot``` provides two forms of facets: ```facet_grid``` and ```facet_wrap```. Using either, we get to split the data further by values in a column. We will use ```facet_wrap``` on ```slice_world``` here:
```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template,
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  facet_wrap(~ slice_world) +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  xlab("Posterior-Anterior") +
  ylab("Inferior-Superior") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.title=element_text(size=10),
        axis.title.y = element_text(angle=90))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + facet_wrap("~slice_world")
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + xlab("Posterior-Anterior")
    + ylab("Inferior-Superior")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(
        axis_title=element_text(size=10),
        axis_title_y=element_text(angle=90)
    )
)
```
![](/multi3.png)
We can also modify the strip titles (i.e. facet labels) directly within the code using ```glue```:

```r
r

ggplot(data=df_template,
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  facet_wrap(~ glue("x = {slice_world}")) +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  xlab("Posterior-Anterior") +
  ylab("Inferior-Superior") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.title=element_text(size=10),
        axis.title.y = element_text(angle=90))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(
        data=df_template.assign(
            slice_label=lambda df: "x = " + df["slice_world"].astype(str)
        ),
        mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"),
    )
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + facet_wrap("~slice_label")
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + xlab("Posterior-Anterior")
    + ylab("Inferior-Superior")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(
        axis_title=element_text(size=10),
        axis_title_y=element_text(angle=90),
    )
)
```
![](/multi4.png)
By default, ```ggplot``` adds a little bit of extra room in the x- and y-axes, helping with not having points at the very edge of the plot. This doesn’t help with raster images though. 

We can override the default x and y scales by adding our own, with the ```expand``` option. Let’s switch to a theme that shows the axes to see the extra space, and then see what it looks like without the extra space:
```r
r

plt_with_space <- ggplot(data=df_template,
```

# Layering stats maps

So far, we’ve only plotted slices of a template image, which would generally form the background of a plot. How do we display statistics on top of this? The answer is to simply add more ```geom_raster``` layers or any other ```geom``` that suits the data and visualization you’d like.

Here, we will add a new raster layer representing a single component obtained using a multivariate data decomposition (data is in df_component1). Unlike the ```geom_raster``` called for the background which inherits the data from the main ```ggplot``` object, we will have to explicitly provide the data alongside the mapping. We’ll also provide the usual stuff to go along with it: a unique gradient colour scale with limits. 

Two things to note here: because we are passing a second scale of the same type (```scale_fill_gradient```), we need to first call ```new_scale_fill()``` so that it doesn’t override the previous fill scale and change the colours of our background image. Second, instead of ```oob=squish```, we are electing to drop values outside of the prescribed limits with `na.value=‘transparent’ (values outside the limits become NAs, which we can make transparent).
```r
r

ggplot(data=(df_template),
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  new_scale_fill() + 
  geom_raster(data=df_component1, mapping=aes(fill=intensity)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(name='Component\nvalue', low='darkred', high='yellow', limits=c(0.3, 0.5), na.value = 'transparent') +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  facet_wrap(~ slice_world, ncol=2) +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing = unit(0, "npc"))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + new_scale_fill()
    + geom_raster(data=df_component1, mapping=aes(fill="intensity"))
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        name="Component\nvalue",
        low="darkred",
        high="yellow",
        limits=(0.3, 0.5),
        na_value="transparent",
    )
    + scale_x_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    + scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    + facet_wrap("~slice_world", ncol=2)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
    + theme(
        strip_text=element_blank(),
        panel_spacing=0,
    )
)
```
![](/layer1.png)
Remember, order matters. Layers are added sequentially in the order that they are called. Changing the order of the two ```geom_rasters``` will result in the background being plotted on top of the stats, rendering the latter invisible.

```r
r

ggplot(data=(df_template),
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(data=df_component1, mapping=aes(fill=intensity)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='darkred', high='yellow', limits=c(0.3, 0.5), na.value = 'transparent') +
  new_scale_fill() + 
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  facet_wrap(~ slice_world, ncol=2) +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing = unit(0, "npc"))
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(data=df_component1, mapping=aes(fill="intensity"))
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="darkred",
        high="yellow",
        limits=(0.3, 0.5),
        na_value="transparent",
    )
    + new_scale_fill()
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + scale_x_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    + scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    + facet_wrap("~slice_world", ncol=2)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
    + theme(
        strip_text=element_blank(),
        panel_spacing=0,
    )
)
```
![](/layer2.png)

Simply switching the ```df_component1``` to ```df_component1_lowres``` gives us a plot with a high resolution background image and the provided lower resolution stats layered on top - no other modifications had to be made!


# Multiple stats maps

It is important to emphasize how important and useful it is to have the data and plotting elements be separated. This means that if we want to plot other stats maps in the same way, for example another component from the same multivariate data decomposition (```df_component2```), all we have to do is just switch out one data frame for another.

```r
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing = unit(0, "npc"))
```

![](/multistat2.png)
Finally, since we are representing imaging data in “long” form where each row corresponds to a voxel, if we want to plot multiple stats maps (here, components) at the same time, we simply stick the data frames together and additionally facet by component. No need to change mappings or scales/axes - just combine the data into one bigger data frame and facet!

```r
r

# Combine the data frames
# First add a new column called Component which we will facet by, and then bind rows
df_component1$Component <- "Component 1"
df_component2$Component <- "Component 2"
df_components_all <- bind_rows(df_component1, df_component2)

# Plot, this time faceting not just by slice_world but also by Component
# We'll use facet_grid instead of facet_wrap, so that columns correspond to components and rows correspond to the different sagittal slices
ggplot(data=(df_template),
              mapping=aes(x=y, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  new_scale_fill() + 
  geom_raster(data=df_components_all, mapping=aes(fill=intensity)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(name='Component\nvalue', low='darkred', high='yellow', limits=c(0.3, 0.5), na.value = 'transparent') +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  facet_grid(slice_world ~ Component) +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_blank(), 
        panel.spacing = unit(0, "npc"))
```
```python
python

# Combine the data frames
# First add a new column called Component which we will facet by, and then bind rows
df_component1["Component"] = "Component 1"
df_component2["Component"] = "Component 2"
df_components_all = pandas.concat([df_component1, df_component2], ignore_index=True)

# Plot, this time faceting not just by slice_world but also by Component
# We'll use facet_grid instead of facet_wrap, so that columns correspond to components and rows correspond to the different sagittal slices
(
    ggplot(data=df_template, mapping=aes(x="y", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + new_scale_fill()
    + geom_raster(data=df_components_all, mapping=aes(fill="intensity"))
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        name="Component\nvalue",
        low="darkred",
        high="yellow",
        limits=(0.3, 0.5),
        na_value="transparent",
    )
    + scale_x_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    + scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    + facet_grid("slice_world ~ Component")
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
    + theme(
        strip_text_y=element_blank(),
        panel_spacing=0,
    )
)
```

![](/multistat3.png)

# Slice locator
So far, we’ve either been showing the sagittal slices with a strip title that contains the x-coordinate at which the slice is located at, or with no slice location information at all. In general, neither are intuitive for people to visualize - it is better to visually depict the locations of these slices. We will do exactly this, by showing the positions of the sagittal slices.

To do this, we need to first visualize a slice in one of the other two dimensions over which we will show these locations. Here, we’ll use the ```df_template_coronal_locator``` data frame which consists of data for one coronal slice, first visualizing it the usual way.
```r
r

ggplot(data=(df_template_coronal_locator),
                  mapping=aes(x=x, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void() 
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_coronal_locator, mapping=aes(x="x", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
)
```
![](/slice1.png)
Next, we’ll show the locations as vertical lines: the ```geom_vline``` geometry is perfect for this. First, we’ll create a data frame containing the positions of these slices (we need to map these lines to *something*).

```r
r

# Create a data frame called locator_bar_locs, which has a column called bar_locations
locator_bar_locs <- data.frame(bar_locations=slice_axis_coordinates)

# See what this looks like
locator_bar_locs
```
```python
python

# Create a data frame called locator_bar_locs, which has a column called bar_locations
locator_bar_locs = pandas.DataFrame({"bar_locations": slice_axis_coordinates})

# See what this looks like
locator_bar_locs
```
Then, we can add the locator bars, either as solid lines…
```r
r

ggplot(data=(df_template_coronal_locator),
                  mapping=aes(x=x, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  geom_vline(data=locator_bar_locs, mapping=aes(xintercept=bar_locations), color='red') +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void() 
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_coronal_locator, mapping=aes(x="x", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + geom_vline(
        data=locator_bar_locs,
        mapping=aes(xintercept="bar_locations"),
        color="red",
    )
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
)
```
![](slice2.png)
... or dashed lines, using the ```lty``` (linetype) option.
```r
r

ggplot(data=(df_template_coronal_locator),
                  mapping=aes(x=x, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  geom_vline(data=locator_bar_locs, mapping=aes(xintercept=bar_locations), color='red', lty=2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void() 
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_coronal_locator, mapping=aes(x="x", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + geom_vline(
        data=locator_bar_locs,
        mapping=aes(xintercept="bar_locations"),
        color="red",
        linetype="dashed",
    )
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(30, 90), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
)
```
![](/slice3.png)
Finally, we can make this all look much better by removing values outside the mask, and a bit more.
```r
r

ggplot(data=(df_template_coronal_locator %>% filter(mask_value > 0.5, intensity > 40)),
                  mapping=aes(x=x, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  geom_vline(data=locator_bar_locs, mapping=aes(xintercept=bar_locations), color='red', lty=1, linewidth=2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', limits=c(30, 90), oob=squish, guide='none') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void() 
```

# Visualizing atlases and labels
First, we need some additional data:

* ```df_template``` (template data)
* ```df_atlas``` (atlas data)
* ```atlas_defs``` (table of atlas label definitions, mapping label number to structure name and acronym)

The imaging data are provided as a “long” data table, as usual. For simplicity, only one slice is provided. For the atlas data, instead of voxel values provided in a column titled ```intensity```, integer values representing labels are provided in a column titled ```label```. These are the same label numbers in ```atlas_defs```.

Take a look:
#
#
#
#

# Overlay an atlas on a template
An atlas is just another type of overlay which can be layered onto the template using an additional ```geom_raster call```:

```r
r

df_template %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', 
                      limits=c(35, 80), oob=squish,
                      guide="none") +
  new_scale_fill() +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=(label %% 8)), data=df_atlas, alpha=0.5, interpolate=F) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Set3", guide="none") +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void()
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template, mapping=aes(x="x", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(35, 80), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + new_scale_fill()
    + geom_raster(
        data=df_atlas.assign(label_mod=lambda df: df["label"] % 8),
        mapping=aes(fill="label_mod"),
        alpha=0.5,
        interpolation="nearest",
    )
    + scale_fill_distiller(palette="Set3", guide=None)
    + coord_equal(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
)
```
![](/overlay1.png)
Above, we’ve used the ```alpha``` option to give the atlas labels some transparency. We’ll make this look even cleaner by removing values outside the brain mask, for both the atlas and the template.

```r
                      guide="none") +
  new_scale_fill() +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=(label %% 8)), data=df_atlas_masked, alpha=0.5, interpolate=F) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Set3", guide="none") +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void()
```

# Annotate labels
Now suppose we want to add text labels identifying atlas regions in this zoomed in plot of the thalamus and its surroundings. How do we do this? You probably guessed it: another ```geom``` layer for text data. 

The geometry is given: we will use ```geom_text```. But to map the text label to data column, we need to have the labels associated with positions.

To do this, we’ll use a two step process. First, we will do left join the atlas data with structure definitions, effectively giving each row (voxel) in the atlas additional columns containing information on the structure with which that label is associated.
#
#
#
```r
r

# Left join the above
df_atlas_masked_filtered_with_defs <- df_atlas_masked_filtered %>%
  left_join(atlas_defs, by="label")

# See what the joined data looks like
# Note the additional columns that now exist in the data frame
df_atlas_masked_filtered_with_defs
```
```python
python

# Left join the above
df_atlas_masked_filtered_with_defs = df_atlas_masked_filtered.merge(
    atlas_defs, on="label", how="left"
)

# See what the joined data looks like
# Note the additional columns that now exist in the data frame
df_atlas_masked_filtered_with_defs
```
#
#
#
If we were to try to add text labels with ```geom_text```, it would be very very messy - ```ggplot``` would attempt to add a text label for each voxel. Instead, we need a second step, where we take all the voxels associated with each label and come up with a single set of x and y values giving an appropriate position for the text label. In our case, we’ll take the median x and y values of all voxels for a given region as the position to use for its text label. This is easily done via the ```tidyverse``` methods of grouping (```group_by```) and summarizing (```summarize```):
```r
r

# Save as new data frame: df_labels
df_labels <- df_atlas_masked_filtered_with_defs %>%
  filter(x > 0) %>%
  group_by(structure_acronym) %>%
  summarize(label_pos_x=median(x), label_pos_z=median(z))
```
```python
python

# Save as new data frame: df_labels
df_labels = (
    df_atlas_masked_filtered_with_defs[df_atlas_masked_filtered_with_defs["x"] > 0]
    .groupby("structure_acronym")
    .agg(label_pos_x=("x", "median"), label_pos_z=("z", "median"))
    .reset_index()
)
```
#
#
#

Now we can add the labels to the plot:
```r
r

df_template_masked_filtered %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', 
                      limits=c(35, 80), oob=squish,
                      guide="none") +
  new_scale_fill() +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=(label %% 8)), data=df_atlas_masked_filtered, alpha=0.5, interpolate=F) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Set3", guide="none") +
  geom_text(aes(x=label_pos_x, y=label_pos_z, label=structure_acronym), data=df_labels) +
  geom_rect(xmin=-10, xmax=30, ymin=-10, ymax=30, fill='transparent', color='red') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void()
```
```python
python

(
    ggplot(data=df_template_masked_filtered, mapping=aes(x="x", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(mapping=aes(fill="intensity"), interpolation="bilinear")
    + scale_fill_gradient(
        low="black", high="white", limits=(35, 80), oob=squish, guide=None
    )
    + new_scale_fill()
    + geom_raster(
        data=df_atlas_masked_filtered.assign(
            label_mod=lambda df: df["label"] % 8
        ),
        mapping=aes(fill="label_mod"),
        alpha=0.5,
        interpolation="nearest",
    )
    + scale_fill_distiller(palette="Set3", guide=None)
    + geom_text(
        data=df_labels,
        mapping=aes(x="label_pos_x", y="label_pos_z", label="structure_acronym"),
    )
    + geom_rect(
        xmin=-10,
        xmax=30,
        ymin=-10,

        color="red",
    )

)
```

# Combine plots with patchwork
Lastly, we can combine the full brain and zoomed-in plots together using patchwork, into one single plot:
```r
r

# Full brain plot
plt_full_brain <- df_template_masked %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', 
                      limits=c(35, 80), oob=squish,
                      guide="none") +
  new_scale_fill() +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=(label %% 8)), data=df_atlas_masked, alpha=0.5, interpolate=F) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Set3", guide="none") +
  scale_x_continuous(name="Left-Right", breaks=seq(from=-80, to=80, by=10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name="Inferior-Superior", breaks=seq(from=-80, to=80, by=10)) +
  geom_rect(xmin=-10, xmax=30, ymin=-10, ymax=30, fill='transparent', color='red') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void()

plt_zoomed_in <- df_template_masked_filtered %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=z)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=intensity), interpolate = T) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='black', high='white', 
                      limits=c(35, 80), oob=squish,
                      guide="none") +
  new_scale_fill() +
  geom_raster(aes(fill=(label %% 8)), data=df_atlas_masked_filtered, alpha=0.5, interpolate=F) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Set3", guide="none") +
  geom_text(aes(x=label_pos_x, y=label_pos_z, label=structure_acronym), data=df_labels_filtered) +
  geom_rect(xmin=-10, xmax=30, ymin=-10, ymax=30, fill='transparent', color='red') +
  coord_fixed(ratio=1) +
  theme_void()

# Patchwork provides / as a shorthand for placing plots vertically
plt_full_brain / plt_zoomed_in
```
```python
python

# Full Brain Plot
plt_full_brain = (
    ggplot(df_template_masked, aes(x="x", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(aes(alpha="intensity"), fill="white", interpolate=True)
    + scale_alpha_continuous(range=(0, 1), limits=(35, 80), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + geom_raster(
        aes(fill="factor(label % 8)"), 
        data=df_atlas_masked, 
        alpha=0.5, 
        interpolate=False
    )
    + scale_fill_brewer(type="qual", palette="Set3", guide=None)
    + scale_x_continuous(name="Left-Right", breaks=np.arange(-80, 81, 10))
    + scale_y_continuous(name="Inferior-Superior", breaks=np.arange(-80, 81, 10))
    + geom_rect(xmin=-10, xmax=30, ymin=-10, ymax=30, fill="none", color="red")
    + coord_fixed(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
    + theme(panel_background=element_rect(fill="black"))
)

# Zoomed-In Plot
plt_zoomed_in = (
    ggplot(df_template_masked_filtered, aes(x="x", y="z"))
    + geom_raster(aes(alpha="intensity"), fill="white", interpolate=True)
    + scale_alpha_continuous(range=(0, 1), limits=(35, 80), oob=squish, guide=None)
    + geom_raster(
        aes(fill="factor(label % 8)"), 
        data=df_atlas_masked_filtered, 
        alpha=0.5, 
        interpolate=False
    )
    + scale_fill_brewer(type="qual", palette="Set3", guide=None)
    + geom_text(
        aes(x="label_pos_x", y="label_pos_z", label="structure_acronym"), 
        data=df_labels_filtered
    )
    + geom_rect(xmin=-10, xmax=30, ymin=-10, ymax=30, fill="none", color="red")
    + coord_fixed(ratio=1)
    + theme_void()
    + theme(panel_background=element_rect(fill="black"))
)

# Convert plotnine objects into patchworklib Bricks
plt_full = pw.load_ggplot(plt_full_brain, figsize=(6, 5))
plt_zoom = pw.load_ggplot(plt_zoomed_in, figsize=(6, 5))

# Use / to place plots vertically 
combined_plot = plt_full / plt_zoom
combined_plot.savefig()  
```
![](/combine1.png)
```r
r

# Plots can also be stacked horizontally using +
plt_full_brain + plt_zoomed_in
```
```python
python

# Plots can also be stacked horizontally using | (or +)
combined_plot = plt_full | plt_zoom
combined_plot.savefig()
```
![](/combine2.png)
Patchwork provides additional options to add titles/tags/captions via ```plot_annotation()``` and layout plots using custom designs ```via plot_layout()```, but that is out of the scope of this tutorial.
